title: Major Private Banks Seen Capping RM Hiring In 2027; AI To Fill The Gaps – Study
excerpt: . Send to a colleague --> Print (subject to copyright) Request Reprint Rights. The report said that "leading" private banks, with Swiss firms at the forefront, are likely to put relationship manager hiring on hold next year; artificial intelligence tools will help fill gaps that this freeze causes. Major private banks will be holding relationship manager hiring steady in 2027, asking AI to pick up the extra capacity instead, according to an annual report from Amsterdam-based banking software provider Backbase. The numbers behind this finding are Swiss, a spokesperson for Backbase said of the report. Swiss private banks reached a record SFr3. 5 trillion ($4. 17 trillion) in assets under management in 2025; costs rose by 3 per cent against revenue growth of 1. 5 per cent, raising the cost-to-income ratio from to 78. 2 per cent from 75. 6 per cent. Consequently, saving an RM’s time is the most obvious place for AI to prove its worth; in 2027 the gap between private banks that can prove what AI delivers and those that cannot will widen, the firm said. Elsewhere, the report said banks that fail to move AI agents from pilot projects into governed, production use risk falling behind next year. The findings are contained in Banking Predictions 2027. The report sets out 10 trends for the year ahead. It finds that 23 per cent of financial institutions already run agentic AI in production. It also finds that 36 per cent of the world’s major banks expect to more than double their AI budgets. The report is among many that seek to measure the impact of AI on the banking and wealth management value chain. The topic continues to make headlines, with the likes of Barclays and HSBC shedding jobs as the efficiencies attributed to AI kick in. (See stories here and here. ) A question is whether the return on the investment in AI is sufficient to cover the capital expenditure. The report expects 2027 to bring tighter scrutiny of AI spending. Of the AI use cases announced by the world’s 50 largest banks, only 30 per cent came with impact metrics. Boards will demand evidence of returns case by case, the report said, and unproven projects will lose funding. “In 2027, every AI line item in banking will have to justify itself like any other investment, with a baseline, a running cost, and a return,” Greg Fahy, chief technology officer, digital banking, at Backbase, said. Governance is the second main theme. As banks move from single assistants to teams of agents, the report argues that written policies will no longer satisfy regulators. It recommends giving individual agents verified cryptographic identities, checking each action in real time, keeping audit-ready logs and being able to switch off any agent on demand. The report also expects agents to reshape operating models, starting in the back office. Agents would prepare the work and staff would make the decisions. On the client side, the report says that 14 per cent of consumers worldwide already let AI select financial providers on their behalf. It predicts that conversational interfaces will displace banking apps. Banks that act for clients with consent, including putting idle cash to work, stand a better chance of keeping relationships before a third-party assistant intervenes. Contributors to the report include McKinsey & Company, technology consultancy Endava, Kosovo-based Jet Bank and Australian business lender Judobank. The report advises banks to start with one high-friction client journey, measure it against financial baselines and build reusable data and governance foundations for later deployments. See more analyses of how AI affects private banking, wealth management and family offices here , here and here.

AI never forgets… are you sure that’s a feature?
excerpt: . We spent years teaching systems when to forget. Delete old records. Minimize personal data. Define retention periods. Honor requests for erasure. Now we are building AI agents specifically to remember. That sounds useful… and it is. An agent that remembers your preferences, previous decisions, customer context, ongoing tasks, or lessons from earlier interactions can provide a much better service than one that always starts from zero. But persistent memory creates a new question:. What should an AI agent be allowed to remember and when should it forget?. AI does not remember everything. Different systems use memory in very different ways. But increasingly, agentic systems can maintain persistent information across sessions: user context, conversation history, goals, preferences, and more, which helps with consistency. The Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) now treats agent memory as a distinct security surface and specifically warns about memory poisoning. This means malicious or incorrect information being stored in persistent memory and influencing future behavior. Its guidance recommends memory isolation, expiration limits, and reviewing sensitive information before it is stored. So, memory is not simply a feature, it’s something that needs a lifecycle. What exactly did the agent remember?. Imagine an AI agent supporting a customer-service employee. During a conversation, it learns that a particular customer is considered high risk. Later, that information influences how the agent handles another request. But a number of questions immediately come up:. Where did that information come from?. Was it verified?. Is it still accurate?. Was it supposed to become part of persistent memory in the first place?. Who can correct it?. This is where memory becomes very different from a traditional database field. Employees may not even know which pieces of information an agent has retained, or which are influencing its future decisions. A mistake can therefore survive the interaction in which it was made. Worse, malicious information may survive too. OWASP describes attacks in which manipulated content persisted in an agent’s memory, which then affects later sessions. Deleting the source may not be the end of it either. Now, consider another scenario. A customer asks for their personal information to be deleted. So, you remove it from the CRM. But was some of that information copied into an agent’s persistent memory, context store, or another component used to personalize future interactions?. If so, deleting the original record may not automatically remove every copy created elsewhere in the AI architecture. That matters because data-protection rules have not disappeared simply because AI has arrived. GDPR includes principles such as data minimization and storage limitation, as well as a right to erasure in defined circumstances. The UK’s Information Commissioner’s Office similarly stresses that AI systems should not keep personal data for longer than necessary simply because it could become useful later. It’s not enough to ask if an agent can remember all of this, the question also includes whether or not it should remember something, for what purpose, and for how long. Memory needs an owner. Before enabling persistent memory for an AI agent, organizations should be able to answer:. What information can the agent retain?. Which information must never become persistent memory?. How long is memory retained?. Who can inspect, correct, or delete it?. What happens when the original source data changes or is removed?. Can we identify which memories influenced an important action or decision?. This is not simply a technical configuration question. It belongs to privacy, security, records management, risk, compliance, and business ownership. Because an agent that remembers can become more useful over time. title: Splendid launches AI business loan finder in Australia
excerpt: . Fintech GenAI LLMs. Splendid launches AI business loan finder in Australia. Tue, 17th Nov 2026 (Today). KAREN JOY BACUDO Finance Editor. Splendid Finance has launched the Australian Business Loan Finder for Claude and ChatGPT. The free tool searches the published lending criteria of 175 Australian business lenders. It is aimed at business owners researching finance options before speaking to a bank, lender or broker. Users can describe their borrowing needs in plain English, including the amount sought, the purpose of the loan, trading history and whether property is available as security. The assistant then returns a shortlist of lenders whose published minimum criteria appear to match the request, along with links to fuller lender profiles. The search spans more than 550 lending products across business loans, lines of credit, invoice finance, asset and equipment finance, and other forms of business funding. The matching process focuses on the specific product rather than the lender alone, using structured data on loan sizes, terms, minimum time in business, revenue thresholds and security requirements. The Melbourne-based broker said the tool does not provide interest rates, assess creditworthiness or promise approval. Results are indicative and based only on published lending criteria. Research stage. Splendid is positioning the product at the earliest stage of the borrowing process, when business owners are trying to narrow the field of potential lenders. That reflects a wider shift, with small businesses increasingly using generative AI tools for initial research rather than starting with a bank or broker. Users do not need to provide their name, contact details or other personal information to run a search. Splendid said the system receives only the search details passed on by the AI assistant, such as loan amount and finance type, and not the wider conversation. The group also said it stores no personal information through the search tool. Business owners who want quotes can request a callback, but no information is shared unless the user chooses to do so. Shaun Johnson, Co-Founder of Splendid Finance, outlined the reasoning behind the launch. "Business owners are already asking AI assistants about finance, but the answers are often general and don't reflect what individual lenders actually require," Johnson said. "We wanted them to get answers grounded in real Australian lending criteria, right where they're asking the question. It's free, and it's built to inform, not to sell," he said. Broker model. Splendid Finance describes itself as a business finance broker and AI lender-matching platform. It works with established businesses across Australia and focuses on non-bank and private lending rather than acting as a lender itself. Its broader platform analyses bank statements and financial information to match borrowers with lenders using both published and unpublished criteria, with brokers advising on each deal. The new search tool extends part of that lender-matching process into the consumer AI interfaces already used by business owners. The launch also highlights how financial services groups are adapting their products for large language model platforms. In this case, Splendid has made the search available through Claude's connector directory and ChatGPT's plugin directory, while also opening the same search through a public MCP server for developers who want to connect other AI assistants. Bhavi Chadha, Co-Founder and Head Broker at Splendid Finance, said the tool could help borrowers understand a market that extends beyond the major banks. "Most business owners only know their own bank, so they don't realise how many non-bank and private lenders there are, or how different their criteria can be," Chadha said. "Seeing which lenders might fit before you apply helps you ask better questions, whether you go direct or work with a broker," he said. Explore with AI. ChatGPT. Lynne Marek Lead Editor. Share Copy link. Email. LinkedIn. X/Twitter. Facebook. Print. License. Add us on Google. First published on. Artificial intelligence company OpenAI last week launched its inaugural digital wallet for use by its ChatGPT agent, enabling it to make purchases by way of the major card networks. It’s one of the first instances in the evolving agentic commerce world of an AI agent using Visa, Mastercard or American Express to automatically pay for a transaction based on initial instructions to the AI agent. Mastercard also announced a first-time airfare purchase last week. The card networks have been working with AI companies to set protocols for agentic commerce, but they’ve all tempered expectations by saying the new bot-driven commerce is in its early stages of development. AI companies and payments providers are racing to set standards for such transactions to help consumers feel comfortable that there will be safeguards when AI agents get their orders wrong, or in cases of fraud. “We’re introducing ChatGPT Wallet, setting a new bar for secure payments by agents,” OpenAI said in a Friday post. “It’s the first wallet that lets agents pay without access to users’ actual card details and that requires a security check for every purchase, while also preserving existing card rewards and protections for eligible disputes. ”. The card networks have also been working with other tech giants to create the agentic technology protocols, but also to set parameters for which companies shoulder responsibility and liability when transactions go awry. Google, with its Gemini agent, and Anthropic, with its Claude agent, are also competing in the agentic realm. In addition, digital payments player Stripe has connected its Link digital wallet to Meta’s Muse agent. The inaugural ChatGPT wallet transaction was completed using tokenized credentials so the agent is unable to see a cardholders’ card information, such as the security code and expiration date. Initially, the wallet feature will only be available to certain ChatGPT users, the OpenAI post said. It will also allow for card rewards and “eligible disputes. ”. Card company executives have suggested AI agents will not be widely used this year, but they have expressed enthusiasm for adding the new channel of commerce. “Innovation starts slowly until it's sudden,” Visa’s president of value-added services, Andrew Torre, said last week at the KBW Fintech Ecosystem Conference. “What you've seen over the course of the last month, or two months is real interest in agentic commerce. ”. “Clients all over the world see this coming and want to get in our agentic sandbox,” Torre said Tuesday at the conference. “There is a lot of consumer interest and, of course, our clients want to be there where their consumers want to be. ”. The ChatGPT wallet transaction is the first Amex agentic commerce integration, enabling card holders to engage in agent-facilitated purchases, a spokesperson for that company said by email. “We're continuing to work with leading AI and commerce partners on additional integrations to bring trusted agentic payments and Amex Membership value into the experiences Card Members are increasingly using,” the Amex spokesperson said. While ChatGPT’s wallet capabilities are landing just as the U. S. year-end holiday shopping season gets started, executives and analysts don’t expect the new commerce to spool up until next year, at the earliest. That’s partly because some significant players involved in digital commerce, including banks and major retailers, are still not ready to participate in AI-based payments. title: From AI ambition to real CX impact: Why transformation must remain human-led
excerpt: . Customer experience has reached an inflection point. Generative and agentic AI are changing how people discover products, request services, make decisions, and interact with organizations. But the defining challenge is no longer whether enterprises can introduce AI into their business. It is whether they can redesign experiences, workflows, and operating models so that AI delivers outcomes people value. This distinction shaped a recent discussion at ServiceNow Knowledge 2026, where leaders from Capgemini, ServiceNow, Sage, and DHL explored human-led, AI-powered transformation in practice. The conversation, moderated by Tim Arkin, DCX Global Head of ServiceNow at Capgemini, brought the findings of the Capgemini Research Institute AI-Powered-CX_April 2026 to life through client, technology, and transformation perspectives. The message for business leaders is clear: success will not be determined by the number of AI agents an organization deploys. It will depend on how effectively AI is connected to the people, data, workflows, and governance required to complete work and improve experiences at enterprise scale. The ambition is high, but the experience remains fragmented. The research, based on a survey of 9,500 consumers and 1,200 senior leaders and front-line staff across ten sectors, shows the pace of change. 68% of organizations believe AI agents could outperform traditional CX channels, while 20% have already enabled agentic AI in some or most CX activities. Additionally, 58%of consumers believe agents could save them time by automating routine monthly purchases and payments. Yet, adoption alone does not automatically improve experience. An organization can automate an interaction while leaving the underlying journey fragmented. It can make one channel faster while simultaneously losing customer context at the next touchpoint. It can also introduce more agents and interfaces while making the overall experience more difficult to navigate. This execution gap is significant. 84% of executives view CX as a core driver of growth, but only 36% report improved sales after acting on CX feedback. Just 23% have a unified CX strategy across channels, 40% identify fragmented journeys as their greatest CX barrier, and 28% transfer context and conversation history seamlessly between online and offline channels. This is precisely where partnership matters. ServiceNow provides the platform foundation to connect interactions, data, workflows, and outcomes. Capgemini brings the industry, process, experience-design, integration, and transformation expertise needed to turn that foundation into measurable business impact. Together, our shared ambition is to help the enterprise run as one, with AI integrated into workflows rather than added as another isolated channel. Begin with the experience, not the AI agent. For Kerry Race, Global People Services Director at Sage, transformation starts by understanding employee journeys. Sage has introduced Now Assist into its people function, alongside a virtual agent intended to help colleagues access answers more efficiently. However, efficiency is only one part of the design. title: Building trust in an AI-driven banking landscape
summary: Customers want AI's speed, but banks still have their trust. Josh DeTar explains how financial institutions can offer both.
excerpt: An article from. Sponsored. Building trust in an AI-driven banking landscape. A Q&A with Josh DeTar, EVP of Evangelism, Tyfone. Published Nov. 16, 2026. By Fintech Meetup. Share Copy link. Email. LinkedIn. X/Twitter. Facebook. Print. Sponsored content. By Fintech Meetup. SPONSORED CONTENT BY. As people turn to AI for money guidance, institutions can keep those conversations grounded in trusted relationships. Josh DeTar discusses building useful AI with accuracy, transparency and human judgment. Trust has always been fundamental to banking. Why does it feel especially consequential for banks and credit unions today?. TD Bank found 55% of Americans had used AI to manage finances, up from 10% a year earlier, though only 18% trust AI to recommend on its own. OpenAI says more than 200 million people ask ChatGPT money questions monthly. Institutions already hold the data and trust people want. Ceding that conversation to AI Assistants can cost them business and erode public perception over time. Credit unions have long differentiated themselves through relationships and community. How can institutions preserve that advantage as more member interactions move into digital channels?. AI could leave a credit union holding the deposit while another service holds the relationship. Local trust matters: 35% cite community involvement as a reason to switch institutions, RivalMind found. But even though locality matters, convenience often wins. But if you pair community connection with AI-enabled tools that make everyday tasks easy, you've got a winning combination. As AI becomes part of how consumers seek advice, make decisions and manage their money, how might it change the relationship between a financial institution and the people it serves?. Banking is shifting from displaying balances to offering guidance. Asking whether they can afford a home or are overspend ing on a car can deepen the relationship. Asked elsewhere, the institution becomes someone else’s data source. Deloitte found 79% of people trust information on their bank’s website, compared with 46% who trust banking recommendations from generative AI. Many institutions are moving quickly to introduce AI capabilities. What should they consider about transparency, reliability and consumer confidence before bringing those tools into the banking experience?. Ask whether AI provides faster, more relevant information or helps complete a task. Ground answers in approved content and account data, and don’t be afraid to admit uncertainty. Disclose AI use, keep a person available and always require approval before action. Where do you see the greatest risks to trust as AI adoption accelerates - whether in data privacy, security, accuracy or the loss of human connection?. For me, inaccurate answers are still the greatest risk. Data exposure is another; recently a tech company CEO’s AI agent posted his bank balances and spending to the company’s general Slack channel. This is why the trust element is crucial: a governed institutional environment with regulatory and compliance standards can dramatically reduce that risk. Could AI actually make banking more human? Where can automation create more space for meaningful member interactions, and where is human judgment still essential?. Absolutely. AI can handle preparation and note-taking, making room for human attention and less judgmental money questions. At one credit union, a member asking how to save for a first home prompted staff to follow up; that member is now buying a home. AI can surface needs, but people should be the ones to make consequential decisions, especially about lending, hardship and major life events. Tyfone is investing in AI-enabled digital banking, including nFinia and Fathom. What problems are you focused on solving, and how does trust shape your approach to building these capabilities?. UniCredit Chief Executive Andrea Orcel said AI was enabling more commercial, higher-value work and greater client engagement. Santander said its AI initiatives generated 194 million euros in business value in the first nine months of 2026, while Chief Financial Officer José García Cantera said the technology was being embedded across the bank’s processes. ABN AMRO is using AI for anti-money-laundering checks and technology modernization while retaining human judgement. Workforce reductions are accompanying the changes. Barclays plans to cut 5,000 jobs, about 5% of its workforce, in 2026; roughly 60% of the reductions will affect support functions, including developer roles. Andrew Stimpson of KBW said cuts have tended to be in back-office and support functions and are only partly attributable to AI. Goldman Sachs plans to constrain headcount growth, while JPMorgan managers have been told to avoid hiring as AI is deployed. Recruiters say banks are increasingly seeking AI, software engineering and data specialists, even as traditional project-management and back-office opportunities decline. Mark Astbury of Morgan McKinley said London’s financial-services sector is becoming a technology employer, and that entry-level roles may become increasingly technical as AI handles more routine tasks. Cost savings and efficiency remain the most common objectives. A September KBW study found customer service was the most frequently cited AI use case, followed by operations, identity checks and financial-crime prevention. Analysts said separately identifiable AI-driven revenue is still difficult to establish, though wealth management and advisory could be an important test as AI may help advisers serve more clients without a matching increase in relationship managers. Uzbekistan's Central Bank develops its own AI solutions
excerpt: Technologies Uzbekistan's Central Bank develops its own AI solutions. Anvar Umarov · 13:40, 16. 11. 2026 · Updated 15:35 · 14 views. Uzbekistan's Central Bank develops its own AI solutions / Photo: UzDaily. Tashkent, Uzbekistan (UzDaily. uz) — The Central Bank of Uzbekistan is developing its own small-scale artificial intelligence solutions and exploring ways to reduce reliance on global providers of such services. Central Bank Deputy Chairman Nodirbek Achilov said this at a presentation of the IMF's regional economic outlook for the Caucasus and Central Asia. According to Achilov, countries across the region, their neighbours and trading partners rely heavily on several major international AI platforms. "All countries in the region, our neighbours and our trading partners currently depend on three or four major global AI platforms operated by large companies. We need to consider how to reduce this dependence," he said. The deputy chairman noted that developing domestic capabilities would require significant investment in local servers and infrastructure. Dependence on one or two providers also creates additional risks to the uninterrupted operation of services. In particular, access to platforms could be restricted by decisions made in the provider's country, while servers might become unavailable when needed. "The expected outcomes should also include scenarios for moving away from dependence on two or three global providers of these AI services," Achilov stressed. He acknowledged that the Central Bank also uses external artificial intelligence services. At the same time, the regulator is developing its own tools to perform specific tasks. "We are not seeking to create a very large, super-AI system, but we can handle smaller tasks ourselves," the deputy chairman said. AI investment and risks for the region. Roberto Cardarelli, Assistant Director of the IMF's Middle East and Central Asia Department, said the issue of dependence on computing capacity for artificial intelligence was examined in a separate IMF report. He said the economic returns on major AI investments, particularly in Gulf countries, would largely depend on demand from foreign customers. This includes whether these countries can export computing capacity to other nations. The IMF's regional economic outlook also examines a scenario involving a sharp correction in the artificial intelligence market. The fund assessed the potential consequences for countries in the Caucasus and Central Asia. For oil-importing countries, including Uzbekistan, the impact of such a scenario would be limited, according to the IMF. The region is not yet closely integrated into the AI development cycle, and the main channel of impact would be a decline in global oil prices. "For oil importers, this is not particularly worrying," Cardarelli said. Share: Telegram Twitter/X Facebook. Anvar Umarov.
